title: Value Nearest to Zero, Ties Go Up
statement:
You get a non-empty integer array nums. Return the element whose distance to 0 is smallest.

If two different values are equally close (like -4 and 4), return the larger one, that is, the positive one.

examples.why: |-2| = 2 is the smallest distance. The answer is the value itself, so the sign stays.
3 and -3 are both 3 away from zero; the tie goes to the larger value, 3.
The closest value can be negative. Picking the smallest non-negative value would give 6.

hints: Compare values by their absolute value, but remember the value itself.
Keep a current best. A new value wins if it is strictly closer, or equally close and larger.
Write the tie rule as a single comparison so you cannot forget it: closer first, then bigger.

explain.intuition:
One pass with a running best. The only subtlety is the tie rule: when |x| = |best|, prefer the larger value. Equal absolute values can only differ by sign, so this just means "take the positive one".

It is the same shape as a sort comparator with a secondary key: first by distance, then by value descending. Writing it as one condition keeps the rule from being lost.
steps: For each x: if |x| < |best|, or |x| = |best| and x > best, set best = x.
pitfalls: Returning the distance instead of the value, which loses the sign.
Keeping the first value at a tie instead of the larger one: [-7, 7] must give 7.
Starting best at 0 or at a huge positive number. 0 is wrong when 0 is not in the array, and a sentinel like Infinity makes the tie rule fragile.

solutions.title: Sort by distance, then value
solutions.idea: Sort a copy by absolute value, breaking ties by larger value first, and take the first element.

solutions.title: One pass with a running best
solutions.idea: Replace the best when the new value is strictly closer, or equally close and larger.

followups: Find the value closest to a target t instead of 0. What does the tie rule become?
The array is sorted. Can you answer in O(log n)?
